dataset.missing_values: No missing values in the diaspora slice or squad file; 8 football rows have NaN scores (unplayed scheduled R16 fixtures, dropped everywhere); WDI tidy files omit country-years with no reported value (Somalia and Puerto Rico have no population rows at all).

ana_01.label: Where the counted diaspora lives: Portugal 52%, France 24%
ana_01.content: The UN's 2024 bilateral matrix counts 146,396 people born in Cabo Verde living abroad -- and that world total is literally the sum of just 24 named destinations, with no 'other' residual. Portugal alone hosts 76,835 (52.5%) and France 34,814 (23.8%): three in four counted emigrants live in one of two countries. The rest of the top six are Angola (9,497), Luxembourg (8,211), Mozambique (7,107) and Italy (5,847). The Netherlands, United States, Spain and Senegal -- major real-world hosts, including the birth country of six squad players -- are structurally absent because those countries' statistics do not break out small origin groups, which is why every number in this table is a floor, not the diaspora.

ana_02.label: Growth 1990-2024: world total x2.8, Luxembourg x7.2
ana_02.content: The counted emigrant stock grew 2.83x in 34 years (51,800 to 146,396) while Cabo Verde's resident population grew only 1.4x. France more than quadrupled (7,645 to 34,814, x4.55). The stand-out is Luxembourg: 1,148 to 8,211 (x7.15), with almost the entire surge in one wave -- 1,617 in 2015 to 7,108 in 2020 -- making Cape Verdeans 1.21% of Luxembourg's total population (677,012) by 2024, the highest density of any destination in the table. Brazil's x286 (5 to 1,430) is a small-base artifact of the 1990 wave.

ana_03.label: Sao Tome: the one big destination that is dying out
ana_03.content: Of 25 destinations, only five shrank between 1990 and 2024, and one dwarfs the rest: Sao Tome and Principe fell from 4,250 (the 3rd-largest community in 1990) to 1,115 (-73.8%), declining in every single wave. This is the demographic echo of the colonial contract-labour system that shipped ~80,000 Cape Verdeans to Sao Tome's cocoa plantations between 1900 and 1970 (det_12): the deportee generation is aging out and no new migration replaces it. The community that Cesaria Evora's 'Sodade' laments is literally disappearing from the table.

ana_04.label: The UN floor alone equals 28% of the resident population
ana_04.content: Even on the strictest possible definition -- born in Cabo Verde, alive, abroad, counted by a destination that reports small origins -- the diaspora has doubled relative to the home population in one generation: from 13.8% of residents in 1990 to 27.9% in 2024 (146,396 counted emigrants vs 524,877 residents). Every heritage-layer estimate (det_07/det_08: ~700k-1M+ including descendants) sits far above this line; the chart of this series should be labelled as the floor it is.

data_table.description: UN counted emigrant floor vs Cabo Verde resident population, per wave

ana_05.label: Top-20 worldwide in emigrants-per-resident, on the floor count
ana_05.content: Reading per-origin world totals from the full UN 2024 matrix and dividing by World Bank 2024 populations, Cabo Verde's counted-emigrant floor (146,396 = 27.9% of residents) ranks #20 of 212 WB-covered origins worldwide, and #2 in Sub-Saharan Africa behind only Comoros (42.4%) -- ahead of South Sudan (26.5%) and Eritrea (25.8%), whose emigration is war-driven. Nearly everything above Cabo Verde is a war economy (West Bank and Gaza 80.0%, Syria 36.2%, Venezuela 29.3%), a Balkan or Caribbean emigration state (Albania 51.2%, Bosnia 50.8%, Jamaica 44.0%, Guyana 56.5%), or a microstate (Monaco 95.0%, Samoa 54.7%, Tonga 51.1%). And Cabo Verde's true position is HIGHER: its four biggest missing host countries (Netherlands, US, Spain, Senegal) are exactly the ones its floor count omits.

ana_06.label: Remittances: 28.2% of GDP in 1980, 12.3% in 2024
ana_06.content: The World Bank series opens in 1980 with remittances worth 28.2% of Cabo Verde's GDP -- the series' all-time peak -- and closes 2024 at 12.3%. The arc is not a straight decline: an 18-19% plateau through the 1980s-90s (1990s mean 18.2%), a slide to the 7.2% low of 2010 as tourism-led GDP growth outpaced inflows, then a pandemic-era resurgence to 15.3% in 2021 (the diaspora sent MORE when tourism collapsed) before easing back. Dependence receded because the denominator grew (det_13), not because the diaspora stopped sending.

ana_07.label: 2024: still #18 of 160 countries on remittance dependence
ana_07.content: Among the 160 true countries reporting in 2024 (WB aggregates excluded via the metadata Region field), Cabo Verde's 12.3% of GDP ranks #18 -- the top 11% worldwide, in a bracket with Uzbekistan (13.7%), Jamaica (16.2%) and Haiti (16.9%), and #4 in Sub-Saharan Africa behind The Gambia (22.0%), Liberia (21.3%) and Lesotho (19.9%). The global leaders are Tajikistan (47.2%) and Tonga (39.2%). Half a century after independence, the diaspora is still one of the economy's main engines.

ana_08.label: Once #2 in the world: 21 straight years in the global top 10
ana_08.content: Ranking every reporting country in every year shows how extreme Cabo Verde's remittance dependence used to be: #2 in the world in its first recorded year (1980, 28.2% of GDP, behind only one country of 90) and again in 1994 and 1995, and inside the global top 10 for 21 consecutive years, 1980 through 2000. The rank then slid to #40 by 2010 as GDP grew, and has since stabilised in the high teens-to-twenties (#18 in 2024). The country's economic history 1980-2024 can be read off a single rank series.

ana_09.label: The squad is the diaspora: 15 of 26 born abroad
ana_09.content: 15 of Cape Verde's 26 World Cup players (57.7%) were born outside Cape Verde: 6 in the Netherlands, 4 in Portugal, 3 in France, 1 in Ireland, 1 in the United States -- a near-perfect map of the emigration destinations, with the ironic twist that the top birth country (Netherlands) does not even appear in the UN's emigrant matrix (ana_01). The imported share is highest in midfield (8 of 12) and defence (5 of 8). The generational sweep runs from island-born captain Vozinha, who turned 40 during the group stage (b. 1986-06-03 -- match reports calling him 39 are wrong by a month), to Portugal-born Wagner Pina (23.7).

ana_10.label: Half the caps, 3 of 4 World Cup goals came from abroad-born players
ana_10.content: The 15 abroad-born players carry 414 of the squad's 823 career caps (50.3%) and 33 of its 75 pre-tournament goals (44.0%) -- so the diaspora contingent is not padding, it is half the team's entire international experience. At the World Cup itself the tilt was stronger: of Cape Verde's four tournament goals, three were scored by players born abroad -- Helio Varela (b. Portugal) vs Uruguay, and both goals against Argentina by Rotterdam-born Deroy Duarte and Sidny Lopes Cabral (det_04); only Kevin Pina's vs Uruguay came from an island-born player. The data also confirms det_04's detail: Duarte entered the tournament with 0 international goals in 33 caps -- his 59th-minute equaliser against the world champions was his first. Counterweight: the record-holder is island-born Ryan Mendes (96 caps, 22 goals).

ana_11.label: Not one of the 26 plays club football in Cape Verde
ana_11.content: The squad's club map is as diasporic as its birth map: the 26 players are employed in 14 different countries, and exactly zero play in Cape Verde's domestic league. Portugal hosts the most (7), then Turkey (3), with Bulgaria, the US, Cyprus and Russia at 2 each, and single players in Romania, Spain, Ireland, the UAE, Hungary, the Netherlands, Finland and Israel. Cape Verde's entire World Cup team is an export product -- even its island-born players professionalised abroad.

ana_12.label: The Elo climb: world #138 in 1998 to #64 -- and an all-time peak mid-World Cup
ana_12.content: Running a standard Elo (K 60/50/40/30/20 by tournament, goal-difference multiplier, +100 home advantage, everyone starts at 1500 -- constants documented in code) over all 49,493 played internationals since 1872: Cape Verde's first recorded match is a 3-2 loss in Gambia in 1959 (one colonial-era friendly), the continuous record starts at the 1979 Amilcar Cabral Cup. The trajectory bottoms at 1383 (world #115) in 1988 and again 1384 (#138 of 198 FIFA-family teams) in 1998, then climbs almost monotonically for 25 years: #108 in 2010, #86 in 2014, #64 by July 2026. The all-time peak rating, 1702, was set DURING the World Cup on 2026-06-26 (after the 0-0 with Saudi Arabia); even after the Argentina defeat the rating (1699) sits within 3 points of the peak. This is the quantitative arc of det_02's 'small nation rising'.

ana_13.label: Win rate by decade: 28% in the 1980s, 43% in the 2020s
ana_13.content: Cape Verde's match record improves decade over decade almost without interruption: 28.1% wins in the 1980s (32 matches), a 23.5% dip in the sparse 1990s (17 matches -- the federation could not afford regular fixtures), then 35.8% in the 2000s, 42.4% in the 2010s and 42.6% in the 2020s. The unbeaten rate tells the cleaner story: 43.8% -> 52.9% -> 62.3% -> 65.2% -> 72.1%. The 2020s cohort (68 matches) is the diaspora-recruitment generation of det_06.

data_table.description: Cape Verde played-match record by decade (1950s = the single 1959 colonial-era friendly)

ana_14.label: The World Cup arc: four matches, never beaten in 90 minutes
ana_14.content: Match by match against the Elo expectations: Cape Verde entered the tournament at 1654 and was given a 3.7% win expectancy against Spain (2219) -- and drew 0-0 (+28 points). Against Uruguay (17.1% expectancy) they came from behind twice to draw 2-2 (+20). The 0-0 with Saudi Arabia was the one dead-even fixture (49.2%). In the Round of 32, Argentina (2225) towered 523 points above them (4.7% expectancy); the 2-3 extra-time defeat cost only 3 rating points. Net: 0 wins, 3 draws, 1 ET loss, group goals 2-2, and +45 Elo across the tournament -- the 'never lost in 90 minutes' record of det_02, quantified.

ana_15.label: Beating Argentina would have been a ~top-25 upset of all time
ana_15.content: Across 33,081 decided matches between established teams (both >=30 prior matches), the largest Elo upsets ever are Luxembourg over Switzerland in 2008 WC qualifying (878-point adjusted gap) and Luxembourg over South Korea in 1980 (767). Cape Verde owns one genuinely historic entry: the 2-0 friendly win IN Portugal in 2015, a 440-point gap that ranks #73 of all 33,081 decided matches -- against the very country that hosts 52% of its counted diaspora. Had they beaten Argentina on 2026-07-03 (523-point gap), it would have ranked ~#25 all-time and #2 among World Cup FINALS upsets ever, behind only Cameroon-Brazil 2022 (gap 534) and ahead of Saudi Arabia-Argentina 2022 (446) and USA-England 1950 (429). They came within nine minutes of it.

ana_17.label: Third-least-populous World Cup nation ever -- verified
ana_17.content: Joining every World Cup participant since 1962 to its edition-year population (415 participant-editions; 2026 uses 2025 populations, the latest): only two teams ever came from smaller countries than Cape Verde's 527,326 -- Curacao 2026 (156,263) and Iceland 2018 (352,721). The story brief's 'second-smallest after Iceland' framing is stale: Curacao's qualification a month after Cape Verde's pushed them to third, exactly as det_03 flagged. Only three sub-1M nations have EVER played a World Cup, all since 2018, two of them in 2026 -- the tournament's 48-team expansion opened a door small nations are walking through. Next on the all-time list: Trinidad and Tobago 2006 (1.30M), Kuwait 1982 (1.66M).

ana_18.label: Smallest nation ever in the knockouts -- by a factor of five
ana_18.content: Using the exact post-1962 rule that a team advanced past the first round iff it played a 4th match in the edition: Cape Verde (527,326) is the least-populous nation ever to do it, and it is not close -- the next-smallest advancer in World Cup history is Uruguay 1966 at 2,707,646, i.e. 5.1x larger. The two smaller participants never advanced (Curacao and Iceland both exited after 3 group games). Scale of the achievement in one line: the average WC2026 participant country has 47.2 million people (median 30.2M) -- 89 times Cape Verde -- and the biggest, the US, is 648 times larger. The det_02/det_03 claim 'smallest nation ever to reach the knockout stage' is computationally verified (with the NI-1982 caveat recorded in ana_caveat_06).

ana_19.label: Cape Verde's chances against Argentina: 3.4% to win, 8.3% to force extra time
ana_19.content: A symmetric ordered-logit model on Elo difference -- fitted to 30,195 internationals 1990-2026, out-of-sample-validated in ana_20, with symmetric thresholds so a neutral-venue prediction cannot depend on which team is listed first -- turns the 523.4-point pre-match gap (Argentina 2225.0 vs Cape Verde 1701.6, neutral Miami venue) into: 3.4% Cape Verde win in 90 minutes, 8.3% level after 90 (i.e. reach extra time), 88.3% Argentina win in 90. Counting a level match as a coin flip, Cape Verde had a 7.6% chance of advancing -- and they landed inside the 8.3% branch, taking the champions to the 111th minute. The model retrospectively rates the group stage as improbable too: 2.8% to beat Spain (drew), 11.3% to beat Uruguay (drew), 33.4% vs Saudi Arabia (drew). Every constant is published and the identical computation ships as pure JS (client_model.js), so a reader can re-run the odds live -- including against any of the 32 knockout teams.

notable_instance.value: 8.3% chance of reaching extra time -- which is exactly what happened
notable_instance.why: The improbable branch the night actually took: the model quantifies how unlikely 'nine minutes from the biggest upset in World Cup history' was.

inputs.rA: Elo rating of team A (use RATINGS_PRE_R32 for any of the 32 knockout teams, or a slider)
inputs.homesign: +1 A at home, -1 B at home, 0 neutral (WC2026 venues are neutral)

client_model.formula: u = B*((rA-rB)/400 + H*homesign); P(A wins)=1-sigmoid(C-u); P(A loses)=sigmoid(-C-u); P(draw)=rest; advance = win + 0.5*draw. Constants C=0.6614, B=2.0468, H=0.2965.
client_model.data_table_ref: RATINGS_PRE_R32 (32 knockout teams' Elo after the 2026 group stage) inlined in code/client_model.js.
client_model.rounding: probabilities to 1 dp. Baseline capeVerdeVsArgentina() -> {win:3.4, draw:8.3, loss:88.3, advance:7.6} -- node-verified identical to the Python output.

ana_20.label: Validation: the odds model beats naive baselines by 19% out-of-sample
ana_20.content: Trained only on 1990-2014 (19,514 matches) and tested on 10,681 fully out-of-sample matches from 2015-2026, the model's 3-class Brier score is 0.5151 vs 0.6346 for a base-rate baseline (18.8% better); log-loss 0.8753 vs 1.0524 (16.8% better). Calibration is tight across all deciles: teams given e.g. a 15.1% win chance won 13.7% of the time, and the maximum predicted-vs-observed gap in any decile is 2.5 points. The underlying Elo expectancy alone scores Brier 0.1284 vs 0.1918 for a coin-flip baseline. LEVEL STATEMENT: this validates PER-MATCH outcome probabilities -- the same level as the ana_19 headline (one match, Cape Verde vs Argentina), so headline and validation match; no tournament-level aggregate is claimed anywhere. What would falsify ana_19: a calibration table where low-probability deciles won far more often than predicted, or a Brier no better than base rates -- neither occurs.

caveats.content: LAYER RULE (binding for every downstream role): all diaspora numbers in ana_01..ana_05 are the UN 'born in Cabo Verde, living abroad' migrant-stock layer -- a FLOOR. The Netherlands, United States, Spain and Senegal are structurally absent from the 2024 bilateral matrix, and the 146,396 world total is literally the sum of the 24 named destinations (no 'other' residual). Never mix these values with citizens-abroad or heritage/ancestry estimates (det_07/det_08/det_10 carry those, with sources); label every chart with its layer.

ana_05's global ratio ranking covers the 212 origins with a WB population row in the shipped file; 21 origins are excluded, largest Puerto Rico (1,948,223 counted emigrants) and Somalia (1,935,594) -- with UN WPP populations Puerto Rico (a US territory, pop ~3.2M) would rank above Cabo Verde and Somalia (pop ~18M) below it. Treat the #20 rank as 'among WB-covered origins'. Emigrant floors are computed on the same UN methodology for all origins, so the comparison is internally consistent.

Football scores are full-time INCLUDING extra time; penalty shootouts are recorded as draws (the 2026-07-03 match appears as 3-2, the three shootout-decided R32 ties as draws). The 8 scheduled-but-unplayed R16 fixtures (2026-07-04..06, NaN scores) are dropped from every computation; all ratings/ranks/probabilities are 'as of 2026-07-03'. The 1959 Gambia-Cape Verde friendly predates independence (1975); the continuous record starts 1979.

The Elo ratings are OUR implementation (constants documented in code/elo_ratings.py headers), initialised at 1500 in 1872 -- levels are not comparable to eloratings.net's published board. Quote trajectories, ranks and gaps computed HERE, never mix with external Elo numbers. Rank pools are restricted to FIFA-family teams (ever played WC or WC qualification) to exclude hobby teams (Jersey, Basque Country) from rankings.

Smallest-nation tables (ana_17/ana_18) cover editions 1962+ because WB population starts in 1960. Historical estimates put every 1930-1958 participant above 1.3M (smallest: Northern Ireland 1958 ~1.4M; Uruguay 1930 ~1.7M), so pre-1962 exclusion cannot affect any sub-600k conclusion. 'Advanced past the first round' = played a 4th match, which is exact for every 1962+ format; note 1974-1982's second stage was a group, not a knockout bracket.

Teams with no WB population row are excluded from ana_16/ana_17/ana_18 tables and printed by the scripts: UK home nations (England, Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland) and defunct federations (Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, German DR). Material case: Northern Ireland advanced in 1982 (and reached the 1958 QF) with ~1.5M people (NISRA estimates, approximate) -- it would rank #2 among small advancers, still ~3x Cape Verde's population, so ana_18's headline stands.

Squad caps/goals are career totals at squad announcement (pre-tournament). WC2026 goalscorer attributions in ana_10 come from detective-sourced facts (det_01/det_02) because international_results.csv has no scorer column; birth countries are country-level only (Rotterdam as both Argentina-match scorers' birth CITY is det_04's sourced detail, not in the CSV).

Age discrepancy vs press reports: the dataset's DOB (1986-06-03) makes captain Vozinha 40 years old at the Argentina match (he turned 40 during the group stage); det_01's Sky Sports source calls him 39. Use 40 -- the data wins.

ana_19's 'reach extra time' reading of P(draw) is approximate: historical knockout matches enter the fit with ET-inclusive scores (shootouts as draws), a small minority of the 30,195-match sample. The 7.6% advance probability additionally assumes a level-after-90 match is a coin flip. The 3.4%/8.3%/88.3% split itself is the validated per-match quantity.

det_03 cites Iceland 2018 at ~337k (a 2017 estimate); the WB 2018 value used here is 352,721. Ordering (Curacao < Iceland < Cape Verde) is unaffected, but quote the WB numbers for consistency with the computed tables.
